Looking past lingering concerns
Focus returns to industry fundamentals
We maintain our target price of W3,100,000 for SK Hynix and recommend increasing exposure. We raise our 3Q26 operating profit estimate to W77tr (from W73tr). With production ramping up at M15X and the transition to advanced DRAM process nodes accelerating, we expect DRAM bit shipments to expand further QoQ in 4Q26. Reflecting this, we also raise our 4Q26 and 2027 operating profit forecasts to W86tr and W396tr, respectively (from W84tr and W386tr).
Recently, investors have sought clarification on potential reductions in HBM specifications, possible one-off costs, and a potential separate listing of Solidigm. Regarding the first issue, we view moves toward replacing 12-high HBM4 with 8-high products in some applications as a way to stretch constrained supply: reducing capacity per stack would allow more stacks to be supplied. With both 8-high and 12-high products already at mature yields, we expect the earnings impact to be limited. We also expect any HBM-related one-off costs to have a limited impact on upcoming results. As for Solidigm, management stated on Oct. 1 that nothing had been finalized regarding a separate listing and that corporate and shareholder value would take priority in any decision. Rather than focusing on concerns about a separate subsidiary listing, we believe the listing speculation itself points to the pressing need for NAND capacity.
Concerns over HBM pricing also appear excessive. Surging conventional DRAM prices have created a substantial margin gap between conventional DRAM and HBM. Unless this gap narrows, suppliers will have an incentive to shift capacity from HBM to conventional DRAM, leaving customers little choice but to accept HBM price increases. HBM3E supplied for big tech companies’ ASICs also has room for price increases in 2027. Accordingly, we expect HBM margins to rise further in 2027 and remain elevated for an extended period.
HBM demand is stronger than expected. With suppliers unable to meet the volumes requested by major GPU and ASIC customers, the industry is bringing forward capacity expansion schedules. We estimate that the share of HBM in SK Hynix''s revenue will expand from around 15% this year to 20% next year. Customers are seeking to maximize the number of compute chips deployed even if this means reducing memory content per chip. This suggests that as memory production expands, the additional supply should ultimately be absorbed through higher memory content per chip.
Shareholder returns are progressing smoothly. Of the W40tr share buyback announced on Aug. 19, over 70% is believed to have been executed, putting it ahead of the original schedule. All repurchased shares are to be canceled. With the shareholder return policy now set at over 50% of cumulative free cash flow for 2025?27, we expect further returns to follow. The company is likely to announce the size and form of its next shareholder return program alongside its 3Q26 results.

Stock Code

An industry first: Quarterly memory revenue likely exceeds US$100bn
Memory demand to outpace supply for longer than expected
We maintain our target price of W400,000 on Samsung Electronics (SEC) and believe now is an opportune time to increase exposure. DRAM shipments slightly exceeded expectations in 3Q26, and we estimate that quarterly memory revenue surpassed US$100bn―a first for the semiconductor industry. We raise our operating profit forecasts for 3Q26 and 2027 to W106.1tr and W537tr, respectively (from W105.7tr and W536tr).
We expect memory supply/demand conditions to be tighter in 2028 than in 2027. A significant portion of 2027 shipment volumes has already been committed, and discussions with customers are increasingly shifting to allocations for 2028. New long-term supply agreements are also being signed at higher prices than existing contracts negotiated under 1H26 market conditions. Meanwhile, supply growth is likely to be constrained by a combination of diminishing gains from process node migrations and an increasing share of capacity allocated to HBM.
Although industry capex is rising, recent investments are directed toward cleanroom capacity scheduled to come online from late 2028 onward. Even facilities slated to come online in 2027 will likely need several more quarters to reach meaningful shipment volumes. According to Micron’s outlook released last week, industry DRAM bit shipment growth is expected to slow to the low-20% range in 2027. These conditions should favor SEC, with its DRAM capacity of 790,000 wafers per month (33.2% of industry capacity).
On the demand side, the recent expansion in agentic AI has increased demand for CPU compute, driving increases in LPDDR, DDR, and SSD content. Server shipments should grow in the high-teens range for two consecutive years. Some customers are limiting memory content per server in order to ship more systems with the available supply, but this reflects supply constraints rather than weaker demand, and the impact on aggregate bit demand should be limited.
Technological advantages in HBM4 and beyond, alongside high dividend yield
We expect HBM prices to reset sharply higher at the start of 2027, narrowing the profitability gap with conventional DRAM. HBM base dies are becoming increasingly important as some functions are moved from accelerator logic chips to the base die to maximize accelerators’ computing performance. SEC’s in-house 4nm base die capabilities could give it a competitive edge in this area.
SEC announced plans to return W90-110tr to shareholders in 2026, with around W30tr in cash dividends expected to be paid in 4Q26. At the current share price, the estimated 2026 dividend yield (including dividends already paid) is 6.5% for common shares and 8.9% for preferred shares. With 2027 free cash flow (EBITDA minus capex) estimated at W519tr, the projected 2027 dividend yield at the current share price would reach 14%, assuming the company maintains its existing policy of returning 50% of free cash flow to shareholders.
